title: The Glory Be
hook: the shortest Catholic prayer, praise to the three persons
carry: as it was in the beginning
tomorrow: The Apostles' Creed, line by line

segments.voice: Yesterday, knees and bows: to genuflect is to bend the knee. Your line was the body says it first. What did your posture say? And today is a milestone. Day one hundred.

Day one hundred. If you've come this far, you've kept at something for over three months, and that deserves a moment. So here's a fitting thing for it: a prayer that takes about seven seconds. Catholics say it so often they barely hear it. It closes every decade of the rosary. It ends every psalm when monks and nuns and priests pray their daily hours. Kids learn it right after the Our Father and the Hail Mary. It asks for nothing. It doesn't confess anything. It just gives glory, and goes back to work. Today: the Glory Be.
screen: `ONE HUNDRED DAYS.` → `A SEVEN-SECOND PRAYER.` → `IT ASKS FOR NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in its traditional English form: "Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen." In the old Latin: Gloria Patri, et Filio, et Spiritui Sancto. Sicut erat in principio, et nunc, et semper, et in saecula saeculorum. Amen. Today's word is the name for a prayer like this: doxology. From two Greek words: doxa, glory, and logos, word. A glory-word. The Mass has a big one, and this is often called the little one. Look at its shape. The first line is the sign of the cross from two days ago, turned from a name into praise: Father, Son, Holy Spirit. The second line is all about time. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be. Past, present, future, in one breath. And that line has a history. In the three hundreds, Christians argued fiercely over whether the Son had always existed or had a beginning. Praying that the glory was the same in the beginning was a way of saying, every day: he always was. So a seven-second prayer carries an old argument, settled into rhythm. The last phrase, world without end, is the old English way of saying forever: in the Latin, into the ages of ages. Catholics use the Glory Be the way you'd use a period at the end of a sentence. After a psalm. After a decade. After a task. It closes things, and hands them back.
screen: `DOXA AND LOGOS: A GLORY-WORD.` · `FATHER, SON AND HOLY SPIRIT.` · `PAST, PRESENT, FUTURE.` · `AN OLD ARGUMENT IN SEVEN SECONDS.` · then, large: `AS IT WAS IN THE BEGINNING, IS NOW, AND EVER SHALL BE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: close something. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you finished today, or will finish soon. A report, a load of laundry, a hard conversation. When it's done, before you move to the next thing, stop for seven seconds. If you pray, say the Glory Be over it. If you don't, simply mark the end: done, and let it go. For now, just sit with the feeling of something finished. The bell holds the time.
Doxology. A glory-word: a short prayer of praise, like the Glory Be, to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Today's word.
Your line: as it was in the beginning. Today, at the end of one task, pause for seven seconds before starting the next. Day one hundred.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Glory Be at the end of each decade of the rosary and after the psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours, and many say it on its own at the end of a task or a day.

trapdoor: what you thought: a quick prayer kids learn by heart.
what it means: a doxology, a glory-word, praising the three persons across past, present and future.
what a scholar hears: the second half is often linked to the fourth-century arguments with the Arians. in saecula saeculorum, into the ages of ages, became world without end.

notes: The traditional English Glory Be is quoted in full in the voice (with 'Holy Spirit'; older Catholic books say 'Holy Ghost'). It is an old traditional text; the cited public-domain English form is the Book of Common Prayer 1662 wording of the same prayer. Confirm the Keeper is happy with this form.
Latin text of the Gloria Patri given from memory; confirm.
The link between 'sicut erat in principio' and the Arian controversy is commonly stated but debated; phrased as 'that line has a history'. Confirm.
'Lesser doxology' (Glory Be) vs 'greater doxology' (the Gloria at Mass): stated as 'often called the little one'. Confirm.
